abstract.text: The paper explores the pernicious effects of excessive use of the go to statement on programming quality and argues for its elimination. It observes that the quality of programmers decreases as the density of go to statements in their programs increases. The author contends that the go to statement should be abolished from all higher-level programming languages (excluding perhaps plain machine code), because it drastically complicates the task of understanding the progress of a process. By examining how processes are characterized using textual and dynamic indices, the paper shows that go to statements make it terribly hard to find a meaningful set of coordinates for describing process progress. The argument concludes that structured constructs like conditionals, procedures, and repetition clauses help maintain a manageable program state description, whereas the go to statement is too primitive and invites messy code. The paper also acknowledges influences and prior observations regarding the undesirability of the go to statement, citing work by Wirth and Hoare, and Böhm and Jacopini.
